all_historical_figures.name: Rāmānuja
all_historical_figures.significance: His advent led to the prevalence of the Pāñcarātra mode of worship in many Śrī-vaiṣṇava temples.

all_historical_figures.name: Madhva
all_historical_figures.role: Vaiṣṇava saint and philosopher, founder of Dvaita school
all_historical_figures.significance: Wrote the 'Tantra-sāra-saṃgraha' and popularized the distinct 'Tantrasāra' āgama tradition, especially in Tulunāḍu.

all_historical_figures.name: Atri, Marīci and Bhṛgu
all_historical_figures.significance: Authors of manuals for the Vaikhānasa tradition of worship.

all_historical_figures.name: Vedānta-desika
all_historical_figures.significance: Shrines dedicated to him are generally found in temples following the Pāñcarātra mode of worship.

all_historical_figures.name: Śaṅkara
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as one of the great saints whose connected days are observed in temples.

all_historical_figures.name: Khāravela
all_historical_figures.significance: His Hāthigumpha inscription claims he organized festivals and gatherings ('uchav samāj') for townsmen.

all_historical_figures.name: Gautami-putra Sātakarṇi
all_historical_figures.significance: The Nāsik cave inscription states that he organised festivals and gatherings.

all_historical_figures.name: Al-Beruni
all_historical_figures.significance: Travelled in India and wrote about the large number of festivals in his book, Kitab-ul-hind.

all_historical_figures.name: Kalhaṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: Described the festival of Śiva-rātri in Kaśmīr as including dancing, singing, and feasts.

all_historical_figures.name: Brahmā
all_historical_figures.significance: Considered the chief participant in the Brahmotsava festival, which is named after him.

all_historical_figures.name: Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Bali, Śiva, Kāma
all_historical_figures.significance: Mythological figures whose great deeds are celebrated in various festivals.

all_historical_figures.name: Sadyojāta
all_historical_figures.significance: A statement ascribed to him is mentioned in the context of Vāruṇa-snāna, describing it as a form of śauca ('cleansing') that purifies the body and aids concentration of mind.

all_historical_figures.name: Nārāyaṇa-kaṇṭha
all_historical_figures.significance: His commentary (Vṛtti) on the Mṛgendrāgama is cited as the source for the statement by Sadyojāta.

all_historical_figures.name: Nārada
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in a quote from Padmottara-khaṇḍa regarding the procedure of 'śauca' (cleansing).

all_historical_figures.name: Bodhāyana
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in a list of revered figures to whom respect is paid during the ācamana ritual.

all_historical_figures.name: Agastya
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in a list of revered gurus after Śiva and Skanda.

all_historical_figures.name: Durvāsa
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in a list of revered gurus.

all_historical_figures.name: Upamanyu
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in a list of revered gurus.

all_historical_figures.name: Merupṛṣṭha
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned as the rishi of the 'oṃ pṛthvīti' mantra for purifying the seat (āsana).

all_historical_figures.name: Īśāna-śiva-guru-deva
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of a 'Paddhati' (manual of worship) which is cited as a source for the classification and ingredients of arghya, gandha, and dhūpa.

complete_timeline.significance: Provided a detailed external account of the numerous festivals celebrated in India.

complete_timeline.date: Around the fifth and sixth centuries
complete_timeline.significance: Made temples popular among the masses, leading to the need for comprehensive temple-lore like the Āgamas.

complete_timeline.event: Earliest probable dating of Āgama texts
complete_timeline.significance: Establishes that the formal codification of temple rituals in Āgamas occurred well after temple worship was already established.
Epigraphic evidence of organized festivals in ancient India.

complete_timeline.event: Impact of the Bhāgavata cult on image-worship and temple-culture
complete_timeline.date: Since the beginning of the Christian era
complete_timeline.significance: Principally responsible for establishing image-worship and temple culture in India.

all_geographic_locations.context: Region where Vaiṣṇava āḻvārs and Śaiva nāyanmārs popularized temples (p.1); location of the Pongal festival (p.13); region where the Mahābhārata provides the background for Navarātri (p.16).
all_geographic_locations.significance: A key region for the development of the Bhakti movement and temple culture.

all_geographic_locations.context: Region (coastal Karnataka) where Madhva prescribed his 'Tantra-sāra' mode of worship for Viṣṇu temples (p.3).
all_geographic_locations.significance: The origin point for the Tantrasāra āgama tradition.

all_geographic_locations.context: Its ritualistic procedures have close affinity with the Tantrasāra tradition (p.3); location of Pūram and Onam festivals (p.13).
all_geographic_locations.significance: A region with a distinct and influential Tantrik ritual tradition.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of the Nav Roz festival (p.13); where Śiva-rātri was celebrated with dancing and singing, according to Kalhaṇa (p.15).
all_geographic_locations.significance: Shows regional variation in festival celebration.

all_geographic_locations.context: Location of the māgh-melā (p.13, 16) and the Kumbha-melā (p.17).
all_geographic_locations.significance: A major pilgrimage site for important festivals.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of the famous Brahmotsava festival (p.13).
all_geographic_locations.significance: A major pilgrimage center known for its grand annual festival.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of the Paryāya festival (p.13, 17); an important center for celebrating Kṛṣṇa's birth (p.16).
all_geographic_locations.significance: A key center of the Madhva tradition with a unique system of rotating priesthood (Paryāya).

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of the Burwā-maṅgal festival and a major center for Śiva-rātri celebrations (p.13).
all_geographic_locations.significance: A preeminent sacred city for Śaivism.

all_geographic_locations.context: Site of the Mahā-mastakābhiṣeka festival, held once in about twelve years (p.17).

all_geographic_locations.place: Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvari, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, Kāveri
all_geographic_locations.context: Invoked during the ritual bath to be present in the water where the bather is, thereby sanctifying it.
all_geographic_locations.significance: These are the major sacred rivers of India, whose presence is believed to make any body of water holy and purificatory.

all_geographic_locations.place: Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Sarasvatī, Narmadā, Sindhu, Kāveri
all_geographic_locations.context: These sacred rivers of India are invoked to be present in the ritual water during dravya-śuddhi (purification of articles).
all_geographic_locations.significance: Symbolizes the purification power of all sacred waters being concentrated into the ritual pot.

all_geographic_locations.context: Mentioned as the source of the best quality sandal-paste (malayodbhavaḥ).
all_geographic_locations.significance: Historically famous for its sandalwood trees, reinforcing the principle that the origin of an article affects its quality for worship.
